A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments auditing and mitigating biases across five reward models, including benchmark accuracies, calibration correlations, and out-of-distribution evaluations.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds best-of-N selection experiments and iterative nullspace projection analyses in Appendices C.8–C.9.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 retains the same difference-of-means probes, final-layer activation extraction, Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization, and null-space intervention. The new AlpacaEval contrast sets change experimental data preparation; INLP is introduced as a diagnostic analysis, not a replacement debiasing method.

E1.justification: v2 adds open-ended AlpacaEval evaluation and best-of-N candidate selection on both AlpacaEval and GSM8K. This substantially extends coverage beyond the retained bias audits and preference-ranking evaluations to selecting generated responses within a prompt.

E2.justification: v1 primarily compares intervened reward models with their unmodified counterparts. v2 adds an actual competing debiasing method, Huang et al. (2025) post-hoc reward calibration, evaluated across all five reward models in both new best-of-N comparisons (Tables 19–20); previously it was only discussed.

E3.justification: The new evaluations introduce 64-candidate selection using Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, disjoint AlpacaEval fit/test pools of 293/512 prompts, and GSM8K pools of 512/807 questions. They add within-prompt Pearson correlations, length-controlled win rates, and selection accuracy. INLP introduces logistic-regression AUC before and after projection, including best one-vs-rest position evaluation. Existing protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix C.9 adds a substantial representation analysis testing whether bias information remains linearly separable after removing one direction, across five bias categories and five reward models (Table 21 and Figure 10). Appendix C.8 also tests held-out selection transfer and contrasts pooled with within-prompt length dependence.

E5.justification: Table 19 adds significance testing of length-controlled win rates against 50%, using AlpacaEval standard errors under a normal approximation and marking significant unfavorable outcomes. Existing bootstrap reporting and the five-percentage-point non-inferiority margin are retained; no increased repeated-run count is established.

E6.justification: Tables 19–21 add substantial new results: AlpacaEval shaping win rates range from 46.23% to 54.42%, and GSM8K mean best-of-N accuracy is 62.76% for shaping versus 62.06% for unmodified models and 61.20% for Huang calibration. INLP adds per-model separability results. Existing tabulated results remain unchanged; Section 5.1 corrects DeBERTa's stated regressive agreement from 60% to 63%, consistent with the retained 0.633 in Table 3.

T1.justification: The probe/projection mathematics and model-style definitions in Equations (1)–(2) are unchanged. The revised taxonomy and INLP discussion provide conceptual interpretation and empirical diagnostics, without new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction narrow the complexity taxonomy toward an empirical distinction between biases tractable or resistant to linear intervention, rather than a stronger characterization of representational geometry. The principal bias discoveries, intervention, and generalization contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of pooled versus prompt-conditioned calibration and interprets INLP as support for the complexity taxonomy. Section 6 newly emphasizes dependence on the reward model and probe-construction dataset, including fresh AlpacaEval probes. The impact discussion also broadens style-bias implications for preference corpora and removes v1's explicit uncertainty about its downstream quality impact.

D1.justification: Appendices C.8–C.9 document the new response generator, longest-two versus shortest-two probe examples, fitting pools, final-layer logistic regressions, and position-classifier selection. Existing experiment details and the stated public code/data access remain unchanged; these are bounded additions supporting the new experiments.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting AlpacaEval, mechanistic terminology, bias substitution, and preference-corpus implications, including Dubois, Saphra and Wiegreffe, and Lamparth et al. It also sharpens positioning against global length calibration. Most existing research positioning remains, and publication/metadata updates do not constitute new cited work.

P1.justification: v2 standardizes model names, corrects wording and cross-references, removes an unfinished editorial note, and locally rewrites the framing and discussion. The impact statement moves from Appendix A into the main text, with subsequent appendix renumbering; the overall document structure remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 19–21 and Figure 10, repositions existing figures and tables, and adjusts labels and captions. The existing charts and principal table structures are retained, so the visual presentation is extended without a substantial redesign.

improvement.justification: The new held-out best-of-N comparisons provide practical validation and an external debiasing comparator missing from v1, while revised limitations clarify probe-data dependence. These benefits are tempered by overinterpretation: Section 4.4 claims all five GSM8K correlations move toward zero, although Table 20 shows an exception, and Table 21 does not cleanly support the claimed simple/complex separation because most style AUCs also approach chance after projection. Overall, the evidence improves, but its interpretation limits the net gain.
